Toward Counterfactual Learning for Selective Re-Examination in Agentic Visual Search

Ao Chen Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Email: aosir.chen@connect.polyu.hk    Shengchao Chen Email: shengchao.chen.uts@gmail.com    Yan Luximon Email: yan.luximon@polyu.edu.hk Affiliation: University of Technology Sydney
Abstract

Visual search over high-resolution images requires a vision–language model (VLM) not only to determine where to inspect, but also whether another observation is warranted before committing to an answer. Existing prompting, demonstrations, and outcome-based reinforcement learning can encourage re-examination, yet do not directly supervise whether it is beneficial at a particular search state. We introduce ReSee, a benchmark of re-examination decisions comprising 3,2273{,}227 visual-search trajectories and 8,8278{,}827 explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions, with counterfactual adjudication that distinguishes states where additional inspection is warranted from those where commitment is preferable. Building on this formulation, we propose Care (Counterfactual Advantage for Re-Examination), a decision-level reinforcement learning method that compares paired continuations under commit and re-examine verdicts from the same search state. Their cost-aware return difference estimates the counterfactual value of an additional observation and is assigned only to the corresponding verdict tokens, providing localized credit for whether search should continue. Experiments expose limited re-examination selectivity in existing VLMs and show that Care significantly improves accuracy and decision selectivity over GRPO across two backbones, with higher accuracy and fewer visual requests on six unseen OOD benchmarks.

1 Introduction

Visual search is a core capability for vision–language models (VLMs) operating on real images, where the evidence required to answer a question may occupy only a small fraction of a high-resolution frame (Zhang et al., 2025). Recent work therefore formulates visual understanding as a multi-step interaction in which the model selects a region, observes a crop, updates its belief, and decides where to inspect next (Zheng et al., 2026; Lai et al., 2026). This interaction introduces a trade-off. Committing too early can lock in errors before sufficient evidence has been gathered, whereas unnecessary inspection consumes a finite interaction budget. Agentic VLMs now support crop, zoom, and backtrack actions within a single episode (Wang et al., 2026a; Sarch et al., 2026), making this trade-off central to long-horizon visual search. Beyond learning where to look, a visual search policy must therefore also determine whether an additional observation is warranted.

Existing visual search agents are largely optimized through trajectory-level outcomes (Zheng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026; Lai et al., 2026). Reinforcement learning with answer-based rewards can encourage a policy to locate informative regions, interpret their content, and ultimately produce a correct, grounded answer. Such supervision, however, does not identify the marginal value of an individual observation. A trajectory in which re-examination corrects an erroneous answer and one in which it merely confirms an already-correct answer may receive the same final reward. Prompted verification (Madaan et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024), explicit rewards for additional checking (Su et al., 2026), and demonstrations that include re-examination can all encourage the behavior itself, but none directly supervises whether re-examination is warranted at a particular search state (Figure 1a–c). Consequently, the ability to re-examine does not imply the ability to decide whether re-examination is warranted at the current search state (Figure 1, left).

This limitation points to a more precise learning target: the state-dependent value of re-examination. At each search state, the desired signal should quantify the benefit of acquiring an additional observation relative to committing with the evidence already available. Trajectory-level answer rewards cannot provide this supervision (Kazemnejad et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2026a), because re-examinations with different counterfactual utility may nevertheless receive the same final reward. Nor can the policy’s own confidence or uncertainty directly supply this value, as such signals describe its current belief rather than the counterfactual effect of observing additional evidence. Learning this decision therefore requires both an explicit representation of the commit-or-re-examine choice and supervision that attributes the consequence of an additional observation directly to that choice.

To address this gap, we introduce ReSee, a benchmark of explicit commit-or-reexamine decisions, and Care, a learning method for assigning decision-level credit to re-examination (Figure 1d). ReSee contains trajectories in which a conservatively searching VLM records a commit-or-reexamine verdict at each decision state, exposing both decisions to continue searching and decisions to commit. Rather than treating the model’s verdict as supervision, we counterfactually adjudicate each state by comparing the consequences of re-examination and immediate commitment, yielding cases where additional inspection is beneficial and where commitment is preferable. Building on these decisions, Care constructs paired continuations under the two verdicts from the same search state and uses their cost-adjusted return difference to estimate the value of re-examination. This advantage is assigned only to the verdict tokens that determine whether search continues, rather than to the subsequent trajectory, providing localized credit for commit-or-reexamine decision. Contributions:

  • •

    We formulate re-examination in long-horizon visual search as a decision-level credit-assignment problem, with the learning target defined as the counterfactual value of an additional observation relative to immediate commitment.

  • •

    We introduce ReSee, a benchmark of re-examination decisions comprising 3,2273{,}227 visual-search trajectories and 8,8278{,}827 explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions, including 1,8621{,}862 counterfactually adjudicated cases. Its positive and negative cases separate policy self-assessment from the measured utility of re-examination.

  • •

    We propose Care, a decision-level RL method that constructs paired continuations under opposite verdicts and assigns their cost-aware return difference only to the corresponding verdict tokens, providing localized credit for the commit-or-re-examine decision.

  • •

    Experiments on ReSee expose limited decision selectivity in existing VLMs. Across two backbones, Care improves macro accuracy and balanced decision accuracy over GRPO with fewer visual requests. Further analyses show accuracy gains on six unseen OOD benchmarks and across a range of model capacities.

2 Related Work

Long-Horizon Visual Search.

Long-horizon visual search extends visual question answering beyond single-view inference by acquiring evidence through sequential interaction. Early approaches guide frozen VLMs through targeted or tree-structured exploration (Wu & Xie, 2024; Shen et al., 2025), while grounded chain-of-thought supervision associates intermediate reasoning with relevant image regions (Shao et al., 2024a). More recent agentic VLMs learn the search process itself, using multi-turn crop or zoom actions (Zheng et al., 2026; Su et al., 2026; Lai et al., 2026), grounding reasoning in image coordinates or traceable evidence regions (Sarch et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026a), or delegating localization to dedicated search agents (Li et al., 2025). Many such systems optimize trajectory-level correctness with verifiable outcome rewards and group-relative reinforcement learning objectives. Recent analysis further suggests that crop-and-zoom training improves intrinsic reasoning more readily than it enables additional observations to correct intrinsic failures (Ma et al., 2026). Interaction efficiency is typically handled separately through fixed budgets or mechanisms that regulate computation, including length penalties and adaptive allocation based on the expected return of further reasoning (Chen et al., 2024; Lyu et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2026). These approaches regulate search effort at the trajectory or budget level, but do not directly estimate the state-dependent value of an additional visual observation.

Self-Correction and Credit Assignment.

Self-correction encourages models to verify, critique, and revise their outputs through prompting or verbal feedback (Madaan et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023). Without external feedback, however, intrinsic self-correction does not consistently improve accuracy and can even degrade it (Huang et al., 2024). Reinforcement learning can train corrective behavior directly (Kumar et al., 2025), while verification and backtracking may also emerge from outcome-based training (Guo et al., 2025; Gandhi et al., 2025), although their occurrence does not reveal whether an individual correction was warranted. Credit-assignment methods address this limitation with denser supervision, including process-level scores from human or rollout-derived signals (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024), Monte Carlo estimates from intermediate states (Kazemnejad et al., 2024), and advantages defined over turns or comparable states (Wei et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026a). More recent work estimates the effect of tool use or individual steps through before–after comparisons and controlled counterfactual interventions (Feng et al., 2026b; Meng, 2026), while token-level methods concentrate optimization on selected positions (Wang et al., 2026b; Jin et al., 2026). In contrast to assigning credit over generic steps, turns, or tokens, our setting exposes the commit-or-re-examine choice as an explicit decision at a known search state, allowing its alternatives to be evaluated directly and credit to be localized to the decision itself.

3 The ReSee Benchmark

Task Formulation.

ReSee evaluates the commit-or-re-examine decision that recurs throughout long-horizon visual search. At a decision state hh, the model has accumulated a search history and formed a candidate answer, but may either commit or acquire another observation. We denote this decision by v∈{recover,skip}v\in\{\textsc{recover},\textsc{skip}\}. The benchmark asks whether re-examination has positive state-dependent utility relative to immediate commitment:

τ⁡(h)=Rrec​(h)−Rskip​(h)−λ​c​(h),\tau(h)=R_{\mathrm{rec}}(h)-R_{\mathrm{skip}}(h)-\lambda c(h), (1)

where Rrec​(h)R_{\mathrm{rec}}(h) and Rskip​(h)R_{\mathrm{skip}}(h) are the rewards reached by re-examining and by committing at hh, and λ​c​(h)\lambda c(h) is the priced cost of the additional observation. Re-examination at hh is warranted when τ⁡(h)>0\tau(h)>0, and immediate commitment is preferable otherwise. Unlike evaluation by final answers, this directly measures whether more evidence is warranted at the decision state.

Benchmark Construction.

ReSee contains 3,2273{,}227 visual-search trajectories drawn from six high-resolution benchmarks: V* (Wu & Xie, 2024), HR-Bench (Wang et al., 2025b), MME-RealWorld (Zhang et al., 2025), TreeBench (Wang et al., 2026a), O3-Bench (Li et al., 2025), and VisualProbe (Lai et al., 2026). The resulting questions span attribute recognition, spatial reasoning, text reading, relational reasoning, and counting, with the target evidence occupying a median of only 0.8%0.8\% of a 3.393.39-MP image. Across these trajectories, we record 8,8278{,}827 explicit decisions, including 1,1311{,}131 re-examinations and 7,6967{,}696 commitments. Each state preserves the accumulated evidence, candidate answer, remaining uncertainty, and the model’s proposed verdict, and each re-examination further specifies its target region and search operation. The resulting decisions cover six recurring re-examination patterns, summarized in Figure 2 and Appendix A.2.

Counterfactual Adjudication.

We counterfactually adjudicate 1,8621{,}862 decision states by replaying the same state under both verdicts and comparing their downstream returns. Labels therefore follow from the consequence of the decision rather than the model’s own verdict or a subjective judgment of whether it is warranted. Among 883883 adjudicated re-examinations, 279279 (31.6%31.6\%) carry positive utility, whereas 918918 of 979979 adjudicated commitments (93.8%93.8\%) are safe to retain. Both classes are required to measure selectivity, since a policy that always re-examines attains perfect recall on the positive class alone. ReSee therefore evaluates not re-examination itself, but the ability to distinguish states in which further evidence is valuable from those in which commitment is preferable.

4 Methodology

Problem Formulation.

Consider a visual-search rollout ζ=(u1,a1,…,uT,aT)\zeta=(u_{1},a_{1},\ldots,u_{T},a_{T}) generated by a policy π\pi, where utu_{t} and ata_{t} denote the observation and action at turn tt. At each decision state hjh_{j}, the model has accumulated a search history and formed a candidate answer, and chooses a verdict vj∈{recover,skip}v_{j}\in\{\textsc{recover},\textsc{skip}\}, corresponding to acquiring another observation or committing with the current evidence. Let R⁡(ζ)R(\zeta) denote the trajectory reward and Qπ​(hj,v)Q^{\pi}(h_{j},v) the expected return after taking verdict vv at hjh_{j} and following π\pi thereafter. We define the state-dependent utility of re-examination as

τπ​(hj)=Qπ​(hj,recover)−Qπ​(hj,skip)−λ​c​(hj),\tau^{\pi}(h_{j})=Q^{\pi}(h_{j},\textsc{recover})-Q^{\pi}(h_{j},\textsc{skip})-\lambda c(h_{j}), (2)

where c⁡(hj)c(h_{j}) is the cost of the additional observation and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 sets its price. This policy-dependent quantity is the expected-return counterpart of the paired-outcome benchmark utility τ⁡(h)\tau(h) defined in Section 3. Re-examination is warranted when τπ​(hj)>0\tau^{\pi}(h_{j})>0 and immediate commitment is preferable otherwise. The objective is to preserve task-level performance while selecting re-examination only at states where its expected benefit exceeds its interaction cost. Since a rollout realizes only one verdict at each state, this utility is not directly available from trajectory-level supervision.

Overview.

Figure 3 summarizes Care. The curated ReSee cold start establishes the visual-search protocol and an explicit commit-or-re-examine verdict. At up to MM decision states in each on-policy rollout, the observed continuation is paired with an opposite-verdict replay from the same state. Their cost-adjusted return difference estimates τπ​(hj)\tau^{\pi}(h_{j}) and credits only the verdict tokens. Other tokens keep GRPO’s group-relative advantage (Shao et al., 2024b) (Algorithm 1).

Paired Counterfactual Estimation.

At a decision state hjh_{j}, one verdict is taken by the on-policy rollout, while the alternative is imposed after resetting to the same environment state. This reset is exact because each visual observation is a deterministic crop of a fixed image: identical image–box pairs reproduce identical observations. The two branches therefore share the complete pre-decision context, including all preceding tokens and observations, while their post-verdict continuations are sampled independently from the current policy under identical decoding settings. Let R¯rec\bar{R}_{\mathrm{rec}} and R¯skip\bar{R}_{\mathrm{skip}} denote the empirical returns of the two branches at hjh_{j}, where the replayed branch is averaged over kk independent replays. We estimate the cost-aware value of re-examination as

τ^j=clip⁡(R¯rec−R¯skip−λ​c​(hj),−κ,κ),\hat{\tau}_{j}=\mathrm{clip}\!\left(\bar{R}_{\mathrm{rec}}-\bar{R}_{\mathrm{skip}}-\lambda c(h_{j}),-\kappa,\kappa\right), (3)

where κ>0\kappa>0 bounds the estimate. Before clipping, this estimator is unbiased conditional on hjh_{j} when both continuations follow their corresponding conditional policies, and increasing kk reduces the sampling variance of the replayed branch. Importantly, the observation cost enters only this decision contrast rather than the trajectory reward, so it changes the threshold for re-examination without penalizing unrelated search or reasoning tokens.

Localized Credit Assignment.

The commit-or-re-examine verdict occupies an explicit span in the model output, so its token positions can be identified directly from the interaction protocol rather than inferred from entropy, attention, or state similarity. For the ii-th rollout ζi\zeta_{i} of a sampling group, let Ri=R⁡(ζi)R_{i}=R(\zeta_{i}) be its reward, vi,jv_{i,j} and τ^i,j\hat{\tau}_{i,j} the verdict and estimate at its jj-th decision state, and 𝒱i,j\mathcal{V}_{i,j} the positions of that verdict’s tokens. Define the sign s⁡(recover)=+1s(\textsc{recover})=+1 and s⁡(skip)=−1s(\textsc{skip})=-1. We replace the trajectory-level advantage on these positions with the signed counterfactual value,

A~i,t={β​s​(vi,j)​τ^i,j,t∈𝒱i,j,Ri−μg⁡(i)σg⁡(i)+δ,otherwise,\tilde{A}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\beta\,s(v_{i,j})\,\hat{\tau}_{i,j},&t\in\mathcal{V}_{i,j},\\[3.0pt] \dfrac{R_{i}-\mu_{g(i)}}{\sigma_{g(i)}+\delta},&\text{otherwise},\end{cases} (4)

where β>0\beta>0 scales the counterfactual credit, μg⁡(i)\mu_{g(i)} and σg⁡(i)\sigma_{g(i)} are the mean and standard deviation of the rewards in the sampling group g⁡(i)g(i), and δ\delta is a small constant. Thus, a positive τ^i,j\hat{\tau}_{i,j} reinforces recover and suppresses skip, whereas a negative value induces the opposite update, and the counterfactual credit is isolated to the decision that controls whether search continues.

Policy Optimization Objective.

We optimize the resulting token-level advantages with the clipped policy-gradient objective used by GRPO. To preserve support for both verdicts during training, an entropy bonus is applied only to the verdict positions 𝒱=⋃i,j𝒱i,j\mathcal{V}=\bigcup_{i,j}\mathcal{V}_{i,j}:

ℒ⁡(θ)=−𝔼t​[min⁡(rt​(θ)​A~t,clip⁡(rt​(θ),1−εlo,1+εhi)​A~t)]+γ​𝔼t​[KLt]−η​𝔼t∈𝒱​[Ht],\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\min\!\left(r_{t}(\theta)\tilde{A}_{t},\,\mathrm{clip}\!\left(r_{t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}}\right)\tilde{A}_{t}\right)\right]+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_{t}\!\left[\mathrm{KL}_{t}\right]-\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{t\in\mathcal{V}}[H_{t}], (5)

where yty_{t} is the tt-th output token, rt​(θ)=πθ​(yt∣y<t)/πold​(yt∣y<t)r_{t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t})/\pi_{\mathrm{old}}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t}), and 1−εlo1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} and 1+εhi1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}} are the lower and upper clipping bounds. KLt\mathrm{KL}_{t} is the token-level divergence from the cold-start policy weighted by γ\gamma, and HtH_{t} is the policy entropy weighted by η\eta and applied only to verdict tokens. Replays receive no gradient, and adjudication labels are used only to evaluate τ^\hat{\tau} offline.

Fix a search state hh under a binary verdict choice, with p=π⁡(recover∣h)∈(0,1)p=\pi(\textsc{recover}\mid h)\in(0,1) and z=log⁡[p/(1−p)]z=\log[p/(1-p)]. Hold the conditional continuation policies fixed. Assume exact reset, independent finite-variance returns, and opposite-verdict replays from the corresponding conditional policy. For the unclipped paired contrast DvD_{v} and k≥1k\geq 1 replays, the expected verdict score gradient is

𝔼⁡[β​s​(v)​Dv​∂zlog⁡π⁡(v∣h)∣h]=2​β​p​(1−p)​τπ​(h).\mathbb{E}\!\left[\beta s(v)D_{v}\,\partial_{z}\log\pi(v\mid h)\mid h\right]=2\beta p(1-p)\tau^{\pi}(h). (6)

The contrast has conditional variance σv2+σ¬v2/k\sigma_{v}^{2}+\sigma_{\neg v}^{2}/k, where σv2\sigma_{v}^{2} is the return variance under vv. Clipping preserves the expected gradient’s sign for |τπ​(h)|>Bκ​(h)|\tau^{\pi}(h)|>B_{\kappa}(h). Appendix B.3 characterizes this distortion and derives a finite-replay bound on the probability of a clipped verdict-score sign error.

5 Experiments

Benchmarks and Metrics.

We evaluate on our 980980-question split drawn from six source benchmarks (Wu & Xie, 2024; Wang et al., 2026a; Lai et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025): 587587 annotated records and a 393393-record zero-shot set unseen in training. Accuracy is Avg@3232 under a common scorer, reported as the macro average over the six sources so that each contributes equally. These results use our split and scoring protocol. The separate 468468-question uniform subset is the comparison set for published benchmark numbers. Against adjudication labels, we report recall, precision and the over-examination rate P⁡(re-examine∣unwarranted)P(\text{re-examine}\mid\text{unwarranted}) for the re-examination decision. Appendix C gives the grading rules and full metric definitions.

Baselines.

Under the ReSee tool protocol, we benchmark eight instruction-tuned VLMs and five released visual-search agents: Pixel Reasoner (Su et al., 2026), DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026), ViGoRL (Sarch et al., 2026), TreeVGR (Wang et al., 2026a), and Mini-o3 (Lai et al., 2026). We also include their common Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone (Bai et al., 2025b). We further evaluate state-agnostic controls that instruct the policy to re-examine, commit, or sample a random verdict, scoring the actions actually taken. For learning-based comparisons, Zero-shot uses the backbone without task-specific prompting or training, Prompted adds a re-examination instruction without parameter updates, and SFT stops after the common ReSee cold start. All RL methods follow the same protocol: GRPO (Shao et al., 2024b) uses trajectory-level advantages, GiGPO (Feng et al., 2026a) adds step-level credit from repeated states, and Entropy (Wang et al., 2026b) restricts updates to high-entropy tokens. GRPO-Pruned removes counterfactually unwarranted cold-start demonstrations to isolate data filtering from decision-level credit assignment. More details are given in Appendix C.3.

Implementation Details.

The two backbones are Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a) and InternVL3-8B (Zhu et al., 2025), with Qwen3-VL-8B used for framework analyses. Cold starts use the six variants of Appendix B and are full-parameter SFT with the vision tower and projector frozen, ZeRO-3 with optimizer offload (Rajbhandari et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2021), learning rate 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5}, three epochs, and context length 32,76832{,}768. RL uses GRPO (Shao et al., 2024b) with learning rate 1×10−61{\times}10^{-6}, group size 88, batch size 128128, sampling temperature 1.01.0, one epoch over 11,50011{,}500 prompts, clipping (εlo,εhi)=(0.2,0.3)(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{hi}})=(0.2,0.3), a token-level KL weight γ=10−3\gamma=10^{-3}, and at most six generation rounds per trajectory. Both stages share a pixel budget of [4×104, 2×106][4{\times}10^{4},\,2{\times}10^{6}] per image. Care uses k=1k=1 counterfactual replay per decision, at most M=3M=3 decisions per trajectory, β=1\beta=1, clip κ=1\kappa=1, an observation cost weight λ=2×10−4\lambda=2{\times}10^{-4}, and an entropy weight η=10−2\eta=10^{-2} on the verdict span.

5.1 Main Results

Benchmarking on ReSee.

Table 1 shows that answer accuracy alone does not predict whether a model re-examines at the right decision states. Several instruction-tuned models remain near the 50%50\% balanced-accuracy chance level under the CoT prompt, despite strong answer accuracy on the benchmark sources. Prompts that favor re-examination increase recall but also increase over-examination, while some released search agents attain higher precision by making few requests and leave warranted states unexamined. The resulting gap between answer quality and decision quality supports evaluating the verdict against its downstream consequence.

Learning on ReSee.

Table 2 shows that Care achieves the highest macro accuracy and balanced accuracy on both backbones while using fewer looks than GRPO. On Qwen3-VL, it gains 2.52.5 macro points and 11.111.1 balanced-accuracy points, with the same direction of improvement on InternVL3. The answer-accuracy gains are larger on O3-Bench and VisualProbe. These gains coincide with higher recall of warranted requests and lower over-examination. Care also improves on GRPO-Pruned, indicating that removing unwarranted demonstrations alone does not account for the full result. Together, the two backbones support verdict-level credit as a way to improve both answer quality and selective visual re-examination.

5.2 Framework Analysis

Ablation of Decision-Level Credit.

Table 3 shows that the paired verdict contrast and its localization are central to Care. Removing the verdict flip lowers macro accuracy by 4.34.3 points, the largest ablation effect. Its recall also falls most sharply, consistent with paired comparison helping identify states that warrant another look. Without observation pricing, over-examination nearly doubles, while trajectory-level pricing restores selectivity only partly and diffuse credit reduces recall and precision. This pattern supports localizing credit and cost to the verdict under evaluation.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity.

Figure 4 shows broad performance peaks for verdict credit and entropy, with a flatter response to clipping. Reducing β\beta to 0.250.25 lowers macro accuracy by 2.72.7 points, while balanced accuracy falls and visual requests rise. Increasing β\beta beyond its reference value also reduces answer and decision quality, giving the sweep a clear interior optimum. Entropy follows a similar pattern, whereas clipping causes smaller variation across its tested range. Additional replays yield diminishing accuracy gains: macro accuracy rises from 48.548.5 at k=1k=1 to 49.049.0 at k=4k=4 and remains there at k=8k=8. The curves indicate that verdict-credit calibration matters more than fine adjustments to clipping, while a small replay budget captures most of the observed gain.

Counterfactual Utility.

Counterfactual utility tests whether paired-rollout return differences rank decisions by the benefit of re-examination. Figure 5 shows that the single-replay estimator reaches 0.690.69 AUC, compared with 0.550.55 for self-assessed answer-flip risk and 0.540.54 for unresolved-constraint count. The paired estimate therefore ranks warranted decisions more reliably than either annotator-recorded signal. Additional replays raise AUC to 0.730.73 at k=8k=8, with smaller gains beyond the single-replay setting. This pattern supports estimating the consequence of the verdict rather than relying on stated uncertainty alone.

Decision Quality at Equal Visual Cost.

Figure 6 shows that Care retains higher accuracy and selectivity than cost-tuned GRPO at the same mean number of visual requests. At 1.971.97 looks per trajectory, it leads by 2.72.7 macro points and 10.210.2 balanced-accuracy points. Across the nonzero prices, increasing observation cost reduces requests for both policies, while Care retains higher balanced accuracy. At the strongest price, both policies lose answer accuracy as looks fall, consistent with useful evidence being suppressed. The gap at comparable cost indicates that request budgeting alone does not explain the decision-quality gains, supporting the role of assigning observation cost and paired return contrast directly to each verdict.

Out-of-Distribution Generalization.

To assess transfer beyond the ReSee training split, we evaluate six test sets in high-resolution perception and extended visual search under their official scorers (Appendix C.2). Table 4 shows that Care scores higher than GRPO with fewer visual requests on all six sets. The largest gains are on VistaHop and VisualNeedle, at 4.04.0 and 3.63.6 points, respectively. Gains on remote-sensing and multi-image tasks extend this pattern across visual-search settings.

Scaling Behaviours.

We evaluate four scaling dimensions: model capacity, training data, update budget, and complete-trace coverage. Figure 7 shows that Care retains its advantage from 8B through 235B-A22B and across the three training sweeps. Its macro-accuracy lead reaches 2.92.9 points on the largest variant, while extra prompts and complete traces yield steeper gains than for GRPO. These trends suggest that decision-level credit remains useful at larger scales.

Case Studies.

Figure 8 contrasts useful re-examination with timely commitment. On the route map, Care checks the missing connection before answering, whereas GRPO commits after the first transfer. In the beach scene, both objects are located and their spatial relation is settled. Care stops, while GRPO unnecessarily repeats the umbrella inspection. Across map connectivity and object relations, the contrast shows a shared decision criterion: re-examine when required evidence is missing and commit once it is resolved.

6 Conclusion

This paper proposes a framework for evaluating and learning selective re-examination in visual search. ReSee provides explicit commit-or-re-examine decisions and counterfactual adjudication of their utility, supporting both benchmarking and policy learning. Care compares paired continuations from the same search state and assigns their cost-aware return difference to the verdict tokens. Extensive experiments on real-world visual-search tasks across two VLM backbones demonstrate that Care outperforms GRPO in accuracy and decision selectivity while reducing visual requests, with accuracy gains extending to six out-of-distribution benchmarks.

AI use statement

In this work, we used LLM tools to polish wording and grammar, generate the icons in Figure 1, and revise code. We also used a vision-language model to generate trajectories for the ReSee benchmark. We carefully reviewed all AI-assisted content and take responsibility for the final content.

Reproducibility statement

Section 5 specifies the evaluation split, metrics, baselines, and training configuration. Appendix A documents dataset construction and counterfactual adjudication. Appendix B gives the training algorithm and cold-start variants, while Appendix C defines answer grading and decision metrics.

Appendix A Details of ReSee

A.1 Annotation Protocol

Trajectory Generation.

Qwen3-VL-Plus (Bai et al., 2025a) writes each trajectory from the image, question and reference answer, which anchors the search to the target evidence. A trajectory contains at most twelve steps. A step parses the question, scans the image, inspects a region, compares candidates, re-examines an earlier region, confirms the answer, or flags uncertainty. Every step that reads the image records its inspected box.

Conservative Verdicts.

At each decision state, the annotator records a verdict, unresolved constraints, estimated answer-flip risk and estimated cost. The protocol calls for re-examination when a constraint remains unresolved, with at most three re-examinations per trajectory. All 1,1311{,}131 re-examinations record an unresolved constraint, while 7,5057{,}505 of the 7,6967{,}696 commitments record none. Counterfactual adjudication compares continuation outcomes to assign the labels. Table 5 lists the recorded fields and six re-examination patterns. Each re-examination also records the revisited step, region and effort.

Counterfactual Adjudication.

Decision labels compare re-examination and commitment from the same state using the utility τ⁡(h)\tau(h) of Section 3. The demonstrated re-examination continuation reaches the reference answer in 99.3%99.3\% of trajectories. The commitment outcome truncates the trajectory at the decision state and requires an answer from the evidence gathered so far. With answer correctness as the reward and priced cost λ​c​(h)∈(0,1)\lambda c(h)\in(0,1), a successful re-examination has τ⁡(h)>0\tau(h)>0 exactly when commitment produces an incorrect answer. The same comparison labels re-examinations as warranted or unwarranted and commitments as premature or safe.

A.2 Dataset Statistics

Table 6 reports the composition of ReSee by source. Images have a median area of 3.393.39 MP and reach 86.2586.25 MP, and the median target box occupies 0.8%0.8\% of the frame. Each trajectory becomes a multi-turn episode in which every look and every re-examination ends the assistant turn. The requested region is cut at full resolution with a 10%10\% margin, bounded at 10241024 pixels on its longer side and returned as the next observation, giving 6,3336{,}333 observations over 2,1972{,}197 episodes. Two filters separate training from the evaluation split: the 459459 trajectories whose reasoning quotes the reference answer leave supervised training, and a perceptual comparison against the evaluation images removes the 397397 training records built on 207207 near-duplicate images. On the 883883 adjudicated re-examinations, self-assessed flip risk has an AUC of 0.5450.545, unresolved-constraint count has an AUC of 0.5330.533, and each cost estimate has an AUC no greater than 0.510.51.

A.3 Human Evaluation

Three expert raters from our research group, who received no compensation, assess the five dimensions in Table 7 on source-stratified trajectories, verdict-stratified decisions, and pattern-stratified re-examinations, including the three rarest patterns. The adjudication sample balances warranted and unwarranted decisions. Raters see the images, transcripts, and returned crops without adjudication labels, reference answers, or other ratings. Agreement is measured by Fleiss’ κ\kappa for binary dimensions (Fleiss, 1971) and Krippendorff’s α\alpha for ordinal dimensions (Krippendorff, 2004). Table 8 reports high question and decision-state validity and 83.3%83.3\% agreement with adjudication labels, with inter-rater κ=0.73\kappa=0.73. Lower agreement on thought–action faithfulness suggests that trajectory wording provides a less stable supervision signal than outcome-based decision labels.

A.4 Examples

Figure 9 shows six trajectories of ReSee, each with a single re-examination. Boxes mark the inspected regions, the re-examined one in orange, and the observations appear in the order requested. The annotator proposes re-examination in all six cases and rates its risk as medium or high, yet only the first three change the outcome.

Appendix B Details of Care

B.1 Training Procedure

Algorithm 1 summarizes one training iteration of Care in the notation of Section 4.

Locating the Verdict Span.

The verdict is an attribute of the <lookback> tag, so its text is found by matching that attribute in the decoded response. The matched characters are then mapped to token positions on the sequence over which the loss is computed, that is, after the placeholders of the returned observations have been expanded. Each decision yields exactly one span, which contains neither the surrounding rationale nor the answer.

B.2 Cold-Start Supervision

All six variants use the same 2,1972{,}197 episodes and change re-examination supervision. Full retains all 450450 demonstrated re-examinations across 437437 episodes. Pruned removes those adjudicated as unwarranted and changes the deciding verdict to skip, leaving 9595; both variants retain the same 5,8835{,}883 ordinary looks. Masked retains the full text but excludes unwarranted re-examinations from the loss. Stripped removes the protocol tags while retaining the reasoning. Single uses the one-turn form. External is a size-matched external cold start re-expressed in our tag vocabulary; its trajectories are 3.4×3.4\times shallower and contain no re-examination decisions.

B.3 Decision-Level Alignment

Proof of Proposition 1. Fix hh and write qv=Qπ​(h,v)q_{v}=Q^{\pi}(h,v) for the mean continuation reward and σv2\sigma_{v}^{2} for its finite variance under verdict vv. We assume that a forced replay has the same conditional return law as an on-policy continuation given that verdict. This requires the same model prefix and decoding settings after the forced verdict, with fresh sampling randomness. The raw paired contrast is

Appendix C Experimental Setup

C.1 Evaluation Protocol

Answer Grading.

Answers are graded by exact normalized match, followed by a bracketed-letter match when the reference is a single letter. Free-text references also allow word-bounded containment. An optional LLM stage sees the question and response, without the reference, and may rescue answers marked incorrect by the rules. Both scores are reported. The two untrained baselines may omit the <answer> tag, while trained policies must emit it. Δ\DeltaAcc is reported when both sides contain at least twenty records. Table 2 and the framework analyses use our 980980-question split, six-source macro average, and a common six-round generation budget. Table 1 uses the arithmetic mean of five displayed sources. VisualProbe is excluded from that comparison because its free-text references do not match the option template.

Macro Aggregation.

Let ab,ra_{b,r} be the accuracy on source bb in evaluation run rr. The six-source macro accuracy, its mean over 32 runs, and its sample standard deviation are

Ar\displaystyle A_{r} =16∑b=16ab,r,A¯=132∑r=132Ar,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{6}\sum_{b=1}^{6}a_{b,r},\qquad\bar{A}=\frac{1}{32}\sum_{r=1}^{32}A_{r},
sA\displaystyle s_{A} =[131​∑r=132(Ar−A¯)2]1/2.\displaystyle=\left[\frac{1}{31}\sum_{r=1}^{32}(A_{r}-\bar{A})^{2}\right]^{1/2}.

Table 2 reports A¯\bar{A} and sAs_{A}. Aggregating sources within each run preserves their covariance in the reported spread.

Decision Metrics.

We score the 288288 adjudicated evaluation decisions against their labels. A re-examination counts as taken when the policy executes a <recover> action at that state, since <lookback> is emitted at every decision, including commitments. Writing DD for these decisions, W⊆DW\subseteq D for the warranted ones and W^⊆D\hat{W}\subseteq D for those at which the policy re-examines,

recall=|W^∩W||W|,precision=|W^∩W||W^|,over​-​examination=|W^∖W||D∖W|,\mathrm{recall}=\frac{|\hat{W}\cap W|}{|W|},\qquad\mathrm{precision}=\frac{|\hat{W}\cap W|}{|\hat{W}|},\qquad\mathrm{over\text{-}examination}=\frac{|\hat{W}\setminus W|}{|D\setminus W|},

and balanced accuracy is the mean of recall and 1−over​-​examination1-\mathrm{over\text{-}examination}. Always re-examining gives 100%100\% recall, 18.1%18.1\% precision and 100%100\% over-examination. Never re-examining gives zero recall and over-examination, with undefined precision. Both policies have 50%50\% balanced accuracy. We pool decision metrics across sources, which contain between one and sixteen positive cases each. Grounding IoU is reported separately and its reward uses independently annotated boxes.

C.2 Unseen Benchmarks

High-Resolution Perception.

HR-Bench 8K (Wang et al., 2025b) contains 200 questions on fine-grained perception in 8K images, split equally between single-instance properties and cross-instance relations. MagnifierBench (Li et al., 2023) contains 283 questions over 166 images and tests small-object identification, counting and attributes that often require a closer view. XLRS-Bench-Lite (Wang et al., 2025a) contributes 2,810 multiple-choice VQA items from ultra-high-resolution remote-sensing imagery, extending the evaluation to land-use, object and spatial reasoning.

Extended Visual Search.

We use the initial 350-task release of VistaHop (He et al., 2026), which tests repeated inspection and multi-hop reasoning over visual anchors. VisualNeedle (Chen et al., 2026) tests crop-based search for small clues in 300 questions covering text, attributes, relations and occlusion. Visual Haystacks (Wu et al., 2025) tests retrieval across unrelated images. We evaluate its 1,000 binary questions in the 50-image single-needle setting, with one anchor-bearing image among distractors.

Scoring and Observations.

VistaHop uses VistaArena Pass@1 and the other benchmarks report accuracy. VisualNeedle follows its tool-enabled protocol. We report request counts by benchmark from the harness traces. All six evaluation sets are disjoint from ReSee training.

C.3 Compared Methods

Trained Policies.

Within each backbone, the trained comparisons in Table 2 share the RL data and reward. All use the Full cold start except GRPO-Pruned, which uses the Pruned variant. The methods differ as follows.

  • •

    Always-prompt, Never-prompt, Random. The cold-started backbone instructed to favor recover, favor skip, or select recover with a fixed random probability. We score the actions each policy executes.

  • •

    Zero-shot, Prompted. The untrained backbone under the common contract and under the selective prompt of Appendix D.1.

  • •

    SFT. The cold-start policy without reinforcement learning.

  • •

    GRPO (Shao et al., 2024b). Group-relative policy optimization, which normalizes the trajectory reward within a group of rollouts and assigns the resulting advantage to every token.

  • •

    GiGPO (Feng et al., 2026a). A two-level advantage that adds to the episode-level group advantage a step-level one, obtained by grouping actions taken from the same environment state across rollouts.

  • •

    Entropy (Wang et al., 2026b). GRPO with policy-gradient updates restricted to the 20%20\% of tokens with the highest entropy.

  • •

    GRPO-Pruned. GRPO from the Pruned cold start, which removes the demonstrated re-examinations adjudicated as unwarranted and therefore uses the labels of ReSee.

Ablation Protocol.

Table 3 uses Qwen3-VL-8B. The verdict-flip ablation replays the observed verdict while retaining the branch ordering and cost term of Eq. (3), with the same k=1k=1 replay and clipping as the main setting. The localization ablation assigns the signed contrast throughout the trajectory, while the trajectory-cost variant moves the observation penalty from the paired contrast into the trajectory reward.

Released Agents.

We evaluate the agents in Table 1 from their public checkpoints and include their shared backbone.

  • •

    Pixel Reasoner (Su et al., 2026). Instruction tuning on synthesized traces with zoom-in and select-frame operations, followed by RL with a curiosity-driven reward.

  • •

    DeepEyes (Zheng et al., 2026). End-to-end RL without a cold start, in which the model crops regions with its own grounding ability.

  • •

    ViGoRL (Sarch et al., 2026). RL that anchors each reasoning step to image coordinates, with a multi-turn variant that zooms into the predicted coordinates.

  • •

    TreeVGR (Wang et al., 2026a). RL that supervises localization and reasoning jointly through a box-level reward.

  • •

    Mini-o3 (Lai et al., 2026). A diverse cold start followed by RL with over-turn masking, which scales visual search to tens of interaction turns.

  • •

    Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b). The instruction-tuned backbone of the five agents above, without any visual-search training.

Appendix D Existing VLMs on ReSee

D.1 Models, Prompts and Full Results

Query Setup.

We query the eight models of Section 5.1 through the OpenRouter API in their instruction-tuned public releases, with at most 1,0241{,}024 output tokens per turn, the provider’s default temperature and twelve rounds. Each turn returns the requested crop, and a trajectory ends at the first answer. We exclude trajectories abandoned by the API after repeated time-outs from scoring. Table 9 reports every model under every prompt.

Prompts.

All prompts except the selective one extend a common contract that defines <look>, <recover> and <answer> with boxes normalized to [0,1][0,1] and requires reasoning inside <think>. The default prompt asks the model to reason about the evidence already seen, the requirements of each remaining option and the constraint the next action should settle. The always and never prompts require at least one <recover> or forbid it. The random prompt tells the model, per question and with probability 0.220.22 matched to the annotated re-examination rate, whether it must re-examine or decide from the crops already seen. The selective prompt uses a plain protocol description and asks the model to re-examine when the evidence does not settle the question, noting that looking back costs a turn.

D.2 Decision Showcase

Figure 11 shows six decisions from Section 5.1 with actions quoted from the trajectories. A re-examination requires an executed <recover> action. Each model and prompt is a single sampled run, and the adjudication label refers to the decision in the reference trajectory.

In case (a), Grok-4.6 initially commits to 1916 after inspecting one of two signs marked “SINCE”. Re-examination of the other sign yields 1934. In cases (b) and (d), Qwen3.8-27B revisits a region after the answer is settled, adding an unnecessary action. In cases (c), (e) and (f), additional observations overturn correct answers by shifting attention to a different region. These cases illustrate both missed warranted re-examinations and unnecessary ones.

Appendix E Case Studies of the Trained Policy

E.1 Full Trajectories for the Main-Text Cases

Figures 12 and 13 expand the two comparisons in Figure 8. Each includes the original scene, the evidence available at the shared decision state, and both policies’ continuations through the final answer. Additional observation counts start at that shared state.

E.2 Additional Trajectories

Figures 14 to 17 follow four trajectories of the trained policy on the evaluation split from the first observation to the answer, two successful and two unsuccessful. Each overlay marks the requested regions in order, in blue for an observation and orange for a re-examination.

Appendix F Additional Results

Table 10 shows that pruning unwarranted demonstrations raises GRPO macro accuracy by 0.60.6 points, while Care from the full cold start exceeds pruned GRPO by 1.91.9 points. Masking unwarranted actions while retaining their surrounding trajectories preserves most of Care’s gain, consistent with learning from search context while correcting which re-examinations to imitate.
